lead: A Linux distribution, or distro, is the Linux kernel packed with libraries, system tools, a shell, an installer and a package manager, so a computer becomes usable after one installation. The kernel alone cannot run your programs; it needs those parts plus a way to fetch more software. Distros exist because assembling all of it by hand is slow and easy to get wrong. You meet them when you format a laptop with Ubuntu, when a server runs RHEL, or when you boot a live USB to repair a machine that will not start.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.3 for the kernel and shell split, and Chapter 1.4 for why the source code is shared.

blocks.text: The kernel is one file plus loadable modules. On its own it can start a processor and manage memory, but it gives you no way to type a command. A distribution adds the missing layers and a program that copies them onto your disk.

items: Kernel: the privileged core; it talks to hardware and schedules processes.
init: the first program the kernel starts, which then starts everything else, usually systemd.
Shell and core utilities: Bash plus hundreds of small commands such as ls, cp and grep.
Package manager: the tool that downloads, installs, updates and removes software in signed packages.
Desktop: optional; GNOME, KDE Plasma or a plain text console.
Installer: the menu-driven program that writes this set onto a disk or a virtual disk.

blocks.text: Only the kernel is common to every distro. Two distros can run the same kernel version and still feel different, because their installer, package manager and default tools differ.

A release is a frozen snapshot of all these parts, given a version number. A long-term-support (LTS) release keeps receiving security fixes for several years without jumping to new versions of the tools. Ubuntu publishes an LTS every two years and supports it for five years. This matters in a lab of 30 machines: you install once, and the same commands keep working for years.
Distros are grouped by the package format they inherit, because that decides which software you can install with one command.

Debian is community-run and favours stability. Ubuntu is built on Debian and adds its own installer, hardware support and release schedule. Fedora is a fast-moving testing ground for RHEL, the commercial Red Hat distribution used on many company servers. Arch ships almost nothing by default and expects you to build the system yourself. SUSE is strong in European enterprise installations.

Package names are not interchangeable. A .deb package belongs to Debian-family systems, an .rpm package to Fedora and SUSE systems. The commands to install them are taught in Unit 4, Package management.
Before any files are copied, the installer asks where Linux should live. There are four common answers.

head: Option
What happens
Existing OS kept?
rows: Linux goes in a separate partition; a boot menu chooses the OS at start-up
Linux runs from the pen drive in memory; the disk is untouched
Linux runs as a guest inside software such as VirtualBox or KVM

items: Pick the language, keyboard layout and time zone.
Choose the target disk or virtual disk. The installer shows a summary of what it will erase.
Create a user account and a password. This user can become root later.
Select the software set: desktop, server tools, development packages.
Let the installer copy files, then reboot into the new system.

blocks.text: A dual-boot machine gives Linux the whole processor and memory when it runs, but only one operating system runs at a time. A virtual machine runs both at once and shares the hardware, so it is slower. In a college lab, one clean install followed by cloning the disk is faster than repeating the installer on every PC.

figure.caption: The worked example as two timelines: 30 separate installs of 25 min take 750 min, while one 25 min install plus 29 clones of 10 min ends at 315 min. The bottom bar is the 435 min (7 h 15 min) saved.

spec.aria: A timeline comparing 30 separate 25-minute installs totalling 750 minutes with one 25-minute install plus 29 ten-minute clones totalling 315 minutes, plus a 435-minute saving bar.

examples.question: A lab has 30 identical PCs that must all run Ubuntu. One clean installation on a PC takes 25 minutes. After that first PC is ready, its disk can be cloned to another PC in 10 minutes per clone, and every one of the 30 PCs needs a finished disk. Compare the time for installing each PC separately with the time for installing once and cloning the rest. Give the saving in minutes and in hours.
steps: Separate installs: each of the 30 PCs takes 25 min. Time = 30 × 25 = 750 min.
Convert to hours: 750 ÷ 60 = 12.5 h, that is 12 h 30 min.
Install once, then clone: the first PC costs 25 min; the other 29 PCs cost 10 min each. Clone path = 25 + 29 × 10.
29 × 10 = 290 min, so the clone path = 25 + 290 = 315 min.
Convert: 315 ÷ 60 = 5.25 h, that is 5 h 15 min.
Convert the saving: 435 ÷ 60 = 7.25 h, that is 7 h 15 min.
examples.answer: Install-one-then-clone takes 315 min (5 h 15 min) instead of 750 min (12 h 30 min), a saving of 435 min (7 h 15 min).

total_clone = install + (n - 1) * clone

print(serial)

examples.question: A single laptop is set up to dual boot Ubuntu and Windows. A student also runs Ubuntu inside a virtual machine on a lab PC that has Windows installed. State two differences between the two setups.
steps: In dual boot, only one operating system runs at a time; the boot menu chooses which one starts.
In a virtual machine, Windows keeps running and Ubuntu runs as a guest process inside it, sharing processor and memory.
Dual boot gives Ubuntu the full hardware; the virtual machine is slower because resources are shared.
Dual boot changes the disk partitions; the virtual machine stores Ubuntu in a disk image file on the host.
examples.answer: Dual boot runs one OS at a time with full hardware and real partitions; a virtual machine runs both OSes together, sharing hardware, inside a disk image file.

traps: A distribution is not just the kernel. Ubuntu and Fedora run the same Linux kernel but differ in installer, package manager and default tools.
Dual boot is not a virtual machine. Dual boot switches between operating systems at start-up; a virtual machine runs the guest while the host stays on.
A live USB is not an installed system. Changes made while running from the pen drive usually vanish on shutdown unless you ask for persistence.
Package managers are tied to families. Do not tell an examiner that dnf installs .deb packages or that apt belongs to Fedora.
LTS means long support, not the newest software. An LTS release deliberately holds older, tested versions of its tools.

quiz.q: Name the four distribution families in the figure and the package manager used by each.
Why can two distributions share the same kernel yet behave differently for the user?
quiz.a: The kernel is only the privileged core. Each distro chooses its own installer, package manager, init configuration, default shell tools and desktop, so the commands and the software sources a user meets are different.

quiz.q: A lab installs Linux on 20 PCs. One clean install takes 30 minutes, a clone takes 8 minutes. Find the serial time and the install-then-clone time, and the saving in minutes.
quiz.a: Serial = 20 × 30 = 600 min. Clone path = 30 + 19 × 8 = 30 + 152 = 182 min. Saving = 600 − 182 = 418 min.

quiz.q: A student wants Windows and Linux on one laptop but must keep all Windows files. Which installation option fits: bare metal, dual boot or virtual machine? Give one reason.
quiz.a: Virtual machine, because it needs no repartitioning of the existing Windows disk. Dual boot also keeps Windows but requires shrinking a partition to make room for Linux.

quiz.q: A company runs the same internal tool on 200 servers. Explain why the administrators might choose an LTS release over the newest release of the same distro.
quiz.a: An LTS release keeps the same versions of libraries and tools for years, with security fixes backported. The internal tool does not have to be retested against new versions every few months, so maintenance cost and breakage risk fall. The newest release brings new features but a short support window.

quiz.q: An examiner says: 'Ubuntu is the Linux operating system and Fedora is a different operating system.' Correct the statement.
quiz.a: Both run the Linux kernel, so they are two distributions of the same operating system family. They differ in the user-space software they bundle, their installers and their package managers (apt for Ubuntu, dnf for Fedora).

quiz.q: What does LTS stand for, and what does it guarantee?
quiz.a: Long-term support. The release keeps receiving security and bug fixes for a fixed, longer period, without requiring an upgrade to new tool versions.

beyond: Not for the exam. Reproducible builds and image-based distributions are changing installation: instead of a long menu, a system image with the whole root file system is written and updated atomically, which is how many container hosts and cloud machines are managed. Fedora Silverblue and similar systems follow this model. Immutable distributions and A/B partition updates are active research and industry topics because they make rollback safe. Search next for 'immutable Linux distribution', 'OSTree' and 'cloud-init provisioning' if you want to see how installations are automated at scale.
